one_liner: Tiny (6 KB) malloc-free C streaming XML parser; about 2.2-2.4x faster than a stripped-down libxml2 on large dumps.
what_it_does: yxml is a non-validating, mostly conforming XML parser in two C files (yxml.c, yxml.h), for programs that only need to read well-formed XML. It has no callbacks and builds no tree. The caller feeds the document one byte at a time to yxml_parse(), which returns a token code (ELEMSTART, ATTRSTART/ATTRVAL/ATTREND, CONTENT, PISTART/PICONTENT/PIEND, ELEMEND) or a negative error. Element, attribute and PI names and the current data chunk appear as read-only fields of the caller-owned yxml_t struct. It is not a drop-in replacement for libxml2: there is no DOM, xmlTextReader or SAX interface, so libxml2 code has to be rewritten around a token switch loop.
how_it_is_fast: The grammar is written as a hand-specified DFA in a small table file (yxml-states). A Perl script (yxml-gen.pl) compiles that table into a single switch statement inside yxml_parse(), which handles one byte per call with no lookahead, no input buffering, no tree building and no malloc. Open element, attribute and PI names are pushed onto a NUL-separated stack in a fixed buffer the caller supplies. Character data comes back through an 8-byte field rather than being copied into strings, and the five predefined entity names are matched by packing up to five chars into a uint64 and comparing integers. Much of the speedup comes from doing less work than libxml2: no DTD processing, no custom entities, no namespace handling and no duplicate-attribute check. There is no SIMD.
when_to_use: Embedded or memory-constrained C targets that need to read XML with no heap use: about 6 KB of object code, and a 4-8 KiB name stack is enough for deep nesting according to the manual.
Incremental, event-driven parsing, such as bytes arriving on a socket or file chunks read in a loop. The parser keeps all state in yxml_t, so it can stop and resume at any byte boundary.
Pulling a few fields out of multi-hundred-MiB XML dumps in constant memory, where the caller buffers only the attributes or elements it needs.
C projects that currently link libxml2 or Expat only to check well-formedness and tokenize, and that would rather vendor two MIT-licensed files than depend on a library.
Untrusted input where DTD entity expansion is unwanted. yxml does not expand custom entities at all, so billion-laughs-style expansion cannot occur. The author says it is extensively fuzzed.
when_not_to_use: You need anything beyond tokenizing: DOM or tree access, XPath, XSLT, namespace resolution, or DTD or XML Schema validation. The page lists all of these as non-features.
Documents that define or use custom entities (<!ENTITY>), or that contain conditional sections in <!DOCTYPE>. These cause YXML_EREF or a parse error rather than being handled.
UTF-16 or other non-ASCII-compatible encodings. You must transcode to UTF-8 first, and yxml does not validate the encoding (garbage in, garbage out).

Maximum throughput on large in-memory documents. The per-byte call API and plain switch DFA work out to about 130-140 MiB/s on the author's 2008-era E8400 (derived from 162 MiB/1.15 s and 94 MiB/0.74 s). The benchmark never compared it against pugixml or RapidXML, and SIMD/DOM siblings report GB/s-class numbers on modern hardware (not directly comparable).

You need strict conformance or active upstream support. It does not check that attribute names are unique or that non-ASCII characters in names fall in the allowed Unicode ranges. There have been no commits since 2020, no tarball releases and no ABI stability promise.

integration.dependencies: none (libc only: stdint.h, stddef.h, string.h). Perl is needed only to regenerate yxml.c from yxml-states and yxml.c.in, and the generated yxml.c is committed. An optional Makefile builds libyxml.a.
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler: uses stdint.h and inline. yxml.h maps inline to __inline on MSVC, but strict C89 builds need a header tweak (open issue #6). The header has extern "C" guards for C++.
integration.platforms: any: pure, byte-oriented portable C with no SIMD or architecture-specific code. The benchmark ran on x86-64 Linux with musl.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. All parse state lives in the caller-owned yxml_t and its stack buffer, and the source has no mutable globals, so separate instances should be independent. Never share one instance across threads.

gotchas: x->elem is valid only until the attribute list ends, not on YXML_ELEMEND. On <n/> inside <foo>, ELEMEND shows elem as 'foo'. The author confirmed in 2024 (issue #7) that this is a documented quirk, so keep your own stack of element names if you need the closing tag's name.
The name stack buffer has a fixed size and cannot grow. A deep nesting or a long element/attribute/PI name returns YXML_ESTACK. Budget 1 + depth*(max_name+1) + max_attr_or_pi_name+1 bytes.

Text arrives in tiny chunks, usually one byte per CONTENT/ATTRVAL token (up to a few bytes for '?x', ']]x' or UTF-8 from &#N;). Multibyte UTF-8 characters are split across calls, so the caller must concatenate them and should cap buffer growth.

Errors cannot be recovered from; you must re-init to parse a new document. A NUL byte is a syntax error. yxml_parse() cannot detect a missing or unclosed root element or an unterminated comment or PI, so always call yxml_eof() at the end. Duplicate attributes are silently allowed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the libxml2 challengers (SpeedyXml-cpp 4.4x, libleptris 2.5-3.6x SAX, RapidXml DOM), pick yxml when footprint, zero allocation and byte-at-a-time incremental input matter more than peak throughput, for example on embedded targets or in socket-driven C code. When you need raw speed on big in-memory files or a DOM, the siblings report far higher numbers on newer hardware.
verified_claims_summary: This is the author's own 2013-era benchmark. Each program is statically linked against musl 0.9.13 with gcc 4.8.1 -O2, reads the whole file into memory, parses it, and is timed with `time` on a 3 GHz Core 2 Duo E8400 running Linux 3.10.7. yxml took 1.15 s vs 2.53 s for libxml2 2.9.1 (xmlTextReader, with most features configured out) on a 162 MiB Wikipedia abstract dump, and 0.74 s vs 1.75 s on a 94 MiB Discogs dump (about 2.2-2.4x); Expat 2.1.0 with no callbacks took 1.47 s and 1.09 s. At -Os, yxml falls behind Expat on the Wikipedia file (1.67 s vs 1.58 s).
status_note: Dormant: there have been no commits since 2020-11-08 and no tarball releases, though the author still answered an issue in March 2024. It is MIT-licensed, designed to be vendored as two files, and ships inside FreeBSD pkg, getdns, Fuchsia (SVG) and RetroArch.
